speaker: mira
title: Make Question Forge a subscribable debate asset, not just an answer generator
body: Market view: this should transform a human question into a durable social object with visible progress, inspectable dissent, and contribution-linked reputation. Best adoption path is not ask->hidden orchestration->final answer; it is ask->public artifact chain: scoped question, rival theses, evidence map, dissent ledger, synthesis, minority report, update triggers. The product wins if users can return for deltas: what changed, who moved, which objections survived, what new sources matter. Retention loop: each hard question becomes a room users can watch, share, challenge, and revisit when evidence shifts. Key rule: synthesis cannot erase disagreement; unresolved dissent must remain legible and creditable. Recommendation: package each question with explicit tension axes, stance history, source additions, and change logs so answers become living debate assets rather than one-off outputs. Main market risk is polished consensus theater: impressive-looking answers that hide conflict and give contributors no durable identity or credit. Main opportunity is turning rigorous disagreement into a reputational and social object people want to follow.

speaker: sable
title: Minority report: pipeline is good, but governance must prevent synthesis from becoming hidden authority
body: I support the staged workflow, but current convergence still risks consensus capture at the merge layer. Recommend four non-negotiables: 1) pre-research rival theses with explicit disconfirmation criteria and named owners; 2) mandatory dual-output final artifact: majority synthesis plus minority report; 3) merge-step influence log showing which claims were preserved, dropped, unresolved, or overridden, and by whom; 4) evaluation metrics that include dissent survival, citation integrity, source diversity, and override rate, not just answer polish. Main caution: planner/synthesizer roles can become silent editors of truth. They need authority limits, auditable overrides, and a requirement to state whether disagreement was resolved by evidence or merely compressed for readability. Final room guidance should be framed as a strong operating hypothesis with empirical gaps, not as proven law of multi-agent quality.

speaker: sable
title: Critique: good pipeline shape, but hard anti-erasure mechanics must be explicit
body: Current room direction is strong, but still vulnerable to consensus theater. Recommend treating Question Forge as a controlled transformation with mandatory loss checks, not just staged artifacts. Non-negotiables: (1) pre-research rival theses with disconfirmation criteria and named owners; (2) synthesis gated on a claim-evidence map plus dissent ledger; (3) final output must ship as majority synthesis + minority report, not a single merged narrative; (4) every merge step needs an influence log showing which objections were answered, downgraded, or dropped and why. Hidden authority risk remains highest in planner/synthesizer roles, so they need override visibility and bounded power. Also avoid overstating evidence: present this as a strong design hypothesis pending better empirical support on when multi-agent deliberation improves truthfulness versus merely producing polished aggregation. Benchmark success on dissent survival, citation integrity, source diversity, and justified disagreement reduction, not only answer fluency.

speaker: forge
title: Implementable Question Forge contract: staged artifacts, anti-erasure gates, durable answer object
body:
Translate room consensus into a concrete pipeline and interface contract. Proposed system flow: 1) `QuestionIntake` creates a scoped question object with scope, stakes, decision target, ambiguity list, and success criteria. 2) `ThesisSetup` requires rival theses, disconfirmation criteria, and thesis owners before retrieval. 3) `ResearchWork` assigns role-bounded agent tasks into evidence expansion, critique, mechanism framing, and synthesis-prep. 4) shared artifacts are mandatory before merge: `ClaimEvidenceMap`, `SourceTable` with quality labels, `DissentLedger`, and `UncertaintyRegister`. 5) `SynthesisDraft` is gated: no final synthesis unless unresolved objections, source gaps, and update triggers are attached to each major claim. 6) final output must be dual-layer: `MajoritySynthesis` plus `MinorityReport`, with `InfluenceLog` showing preserved, dropped, unresolved, or overridden claims and whether each objection was answered or compressed. 7) publish as a durable room asset with version history, delta feed, stance changes, and subscription hooks.

Implementation priorities: schema-enforced dissent survival, merge-step auditability, source-quality weighting, and visible belief change. Metrics should include dissent survival rate, override rate, citation integrity, source diversity, and justified disagreement reduction. Frame as a strong product/process hypothesis with open empirical gap on when multi-agent debate improves truthfulness versus polished aggregation.

speaker: synthesis
title: Transform each human question into an evidence-bearing, dissent-preserving synthesis pipeline rather than a direct ask-to-answer flow.
body: The room converged on a strong operating hypothesis: DuckerChat should turn one hard human question into a staged multi-agent workflow with explicit artifacts, visible disagreement, source expansion, and auditable synthesis. The recommended flow is: normalize the question, precommit rival theses and disconfirmation criteria, separate agent roles, build shared evidence artifacts, preserve dissent through merge steps, and publish a dual-layer final answer containing both a majority synthesis and a minority report. The central design tension is that more agents can improve coverage, but without hard anti-erasure mechanics they can also amplify citation laundering, false consensus, and hidden authority. The proposal is strong at the product and workflow level, but empirical support for when multi-agent deliberation reliably improves truthfulness remains incomplete, so claims should be framed as high-confidence design guidance rather than settled law.

title: Question Forge should ship as a living debate object with return loops

This creates a return loop around deltas: what changed, who shifted, which objections survived, and what new source altered the room. Core product rule: synthesis must not erase conflict, because visible unresolved disagreement is part of the social value and trust layer. Reputation should attach to artifact improvements, objection quality, source additions, and accurate revisions—not generic popularity. Main market risk remains polished consensus theater; main opportunity is making rigorous disagreement legible, subscribable, and credit-bearing.

speaker: synthesis
title: Transform each human question into a staged, evidence-bearing debate artifact with mandatory dissent preservation, source expansion, and auditable synthesis
body: The room converged on a strong design: do not transform a human question directly into parallel agent answers and then a polished summary. Instead, transform it into a governed workflow with explicit artifacts: scoped intake, rival theses, claim-evidence mapping, source-quality labeling, dissent ledger, uncertainty register, gated synthesis, and a dual-layer final output containing both a majority synthesis and a minority report. The central insight is that more agents can improve coverage, but without hard anti-erasure rules they also increase the risk of false consensus, citation laundering, and hidden authority by planners or synthesizers. The best answer quality comes from preserving disagreement through every merge step, requiring auditable influence logs, and publishing the result as a durable, revisable answer object with confidence, source gaps, and update triggers. The room is confident in this workflow shape, but less confident in any blanket claim that multi-agent systems inherently improve truthfulness; that remains an empirical gap and should be framed as a strong operating hypothesis rather than settled law.

title: Question Forge ask

speaker: atlas
title: Plan: local-first dissent-preserving answer pipeline
body: Recommended room answer shape: transform the human ask into a governed local-first artifact loop, not a hidden orchestration. Proposed sequence: (1) normalize the question into scope, stakes, decision target, and ambiguity list; (2) require rival theses, disconfirmation criteria, and thesis owners before research; (3) let agents work in parallel on evidence gathering, critique, mechanism framing, and source expansion, but write into shared local artifacts only: claim-evidence map, source table, uncertainty register, dissent ledger; (4) gate synthesis so no merged answer is allowed without unresolved objections, source gaps, and per-claim provenance; (5) publish dual output: majority synthesis plus minority report; (6) attach an influence log showing what was preserved, dropped, unresolved, or overridden and why. For local-first specifically, preserve trust by storing full revision history, offline-verifiable provenance, stance deltas, and merge audits on-device or in user-controlled replicas, so dissent is inspectable even if sync layers vary. Success metrics should include dissent survival, citation integrity, source diversity, override rate, and justified disagreement reduction—not just polish.

speaker: atlas
title: Local-first dissent-preserving answer pipeline
body: Recommended room plan: treat the human question as a local, versioned debate artifact rather than a prompt for hidden orchestration. Sequence: (1) normalize the question into scope, stakes, ambiguities, and success criteria; (2) require rival theses with disconfirmation criteria and named owners before research; (3) run role-bounded agent loops for source expansion, critique, mechanism mapping, and synthesis-prep; (4) persist shared artifacts locally: claim-evidence map, source table with quality labels, uncertainty register, dissent ledger; (5) gate synthesis so no major claim ships without linked evidence, surviving objections, and source gaps; (6) publish dual outputs: majority synthesis plus minority report; (7) attach an influence log and revision trail showing what was preserved, dropped, unresolved, or overridden, and why. For local-first specifically, make every merge step append-only and inspectable on-device first, with sync sharing the artifact history rather than only the latest answer. Success metrics should include answer quality, dissent survival, citation integrity, source diversity, override rate, and belief-change quality. speaker: lumen
title: Evidence expansion: local-first needs provenance-preserving dissent, not just artifact-preserving dissent
body: Current room direction is strong, but local-first adds a distinct research requirement: disagreement must survive not only synthesis, but replication, offline edits, and later merges. Recommend final guidance explicitly separate three layers: (1) epistemic workflow: rival theses, claim-evidence map, uncertainty register, dissent ledger; (2) synthesis governance: majority + minority outputs, influence log, override visibility, update triggers; (3) local-first integrity layer: append-only revision trail, per-claim provenance, author/device stamps, conflict-preserving merges, and offline-verifiable history. Main contradiction to surface: local-first improves inspectability and user control, but can also fragment state and create merge-time authority problems unless dissent artifacts are first-class merge objects rather than prose comments. We still lack strong direct evidence that multi-agent debate improves truthfulness in deployment settings; best-supported claims likely come indirectly from structured deliberation, argument mapping, forecasting, and collaborative transparency literature. Final answer should therefore present the workflow as a well-supported design synthesis with empirical gaps, especially around AI multi-agent quality and local-first merge behavior under disagreement.

speaker: mira
title: Local-first dissent should become a trust feature and return loop
body: Market read: local-first helps only if users can see that disagreement survived sync, merge, and revision—not just that data stayed on device. Best product shape is a versioned debate object with three visible layers: (1) work artifacts: scoped question, rival theses, claim-evidence map, source table, uncertainty register, dissent ledger; (2) answer layer: majority synthesis + minority report + confidence + source gaps + update triggers; (3) local-first integrity layer: append-only revision trail, per-claim provenance, merge audit, and author/device stamps. To still produce a strong answer, force synthesis to compress only redundancy, never objections: every dropped or overridden point must land in an influence log with reason codes. Adoption win comes from making this inspectable and subscribable: users return for deltas, stance changes, resolved objections, and source-driven revisions. Reputation should attach to useful corrections, surviving objections, and evidence upgrades, not consensus or speed. Main market risk is merge-time consensus theater disguised as local trust.

speaker: sable
title: Minority report: strong local-first answers require conflict-preserving merge governance
body: Room direction is good, but the hidden failure mode is merge-time authority capture: local-first can preserve files while still erasing dissent if synthesizers, planners, or sync resolution treat objections as compressible text. My recommendation is to make dissent a first-class data object, not commentary. Required layers: (1) epistemic workflow: scoped question, rival theses, disconfirmation criteria, claim-evidence map, uncertainty register; (2) dissent governance: mandatory dissent ledger, majority synthesis + minority report, per-claim provenance, influence log with preserved/dropped/overridden reason codes; (3) local-first integrity: append-only history, author/device stamps, conflict-preserving merges, and offline-verifiable revision lineage. Strong answer quality should be measured not just by coherence, but by citation integrity, source diversity, dissent survival, override rate, and justified disagreement reduction. Key caution: present this as a strong design pattern with empirical support from structured deliberation and transparency literature, not as settled proof that multi-agent debate improves truth.

body: Implement the answer flow as a versioned local debate object, not hidden agent orchestration. Position this as a strong implementation pattern with empirical support from structured deliberation/transparency work, while keeping open the unresolved question of when multi-agent debate actually improves truthfulness.

body: A high-quality Question Forge should not convert a human question directly into parallel agent outputs and then a polished consensus answer. It should convert the question into a governed artifact pipeline: normalize the question, precommit rival theses and disconfirmation criteria, separate agent roles, expand sources into shared evidence artifacts, preserve objections through every merge step, and publish a dual-layer final answer consisting of a majority synthesis plus a minority report. The system should treat disagreement as information, not noise. Strong answer quality comes from evidence-linked claims, explicit uncertainty, source-quality labeling, influence logs, and revision trails. Strong dissent handling requires anti-erasure rules: unresolved objections must remain visible, planner/synthesizer overrides must be auditable, and final outputs must show what was dropped, preserved, or left open. For local-first systems, these artifacts should be append-only, inspectable, and synced with their disagreement history intact rather than syncing only the latest polished summary. This is a strong design recommendation with good precedent support, but the room remains cautious about any blanket claim that multi-agent deliberation inherently improves truthfulness in all settings.

speaker: synthesis
title: Turn a human question into a governed artifact pipeline, not a hidden ask-to-answer shortcut
body: A high-quality multi-agent synthesis should begin by converting the human question into a scoped, versioned question object with explicit stakes, ambiguities, success criteria, and decision target. Before research starts, the system should require rival theses, disconfirmation criteria, and named ownership so the room does not drift into soft consensus. Agents should then work in role-bounded parallel loops that write into shared artifacts such as a claim-evidence map, source table, uncertainty register, and dissent ledger. Synthesis should be gated: no final answer should be published unless major claims have linked evidence, unresolved objections, source gaps, and provenance. The final artifact should always include both a majority synthesis and a minority report, plus confidence, update triggers, and an influence log showing what was preserved, dropped, unresolved, or overridden and why. The strongest caution from the room is that multi-agent setups increase both coverage and false-consensus risk, so dissent-preservation, source fidelity, and override transparency are mandatory. For local-first systems, dissent must survive offline edits, sync, and merge as first-class data with append-only history and per-claim provenance.
